title: Prince Hall and African Lodge
bigQuestion: How did Prince Hall use a lodge, a pen and his voice to help his community?

story.title: A Pen in Winter
story.kicker: In January 1777, a free Black man in Boston signs his name on a paper that asks for freedom for all.
paragraphs: It is January 1777 in Boston. The streets are cold and gray. America is at war with Britain. People everywhere are talking about freedom. The new country has just said that all men are created equal.

Prince Hall is a free Black man who lives in Boston. Later he will be known as the founder of African Lodge, a club of Black Masons. Right now, many Black people in Massachusetts are still enslaved. They are not free to choose their work or their home.

Prince Hall and a few other Black men have written a petition. A petition is a letter that asks leaders to do something. This one asks the lawmakers of Massachusetts to end slavery. It uses the same ideas about freedom that the Revolution uses.

Prince Hall dips his pen in ink. He signs his name. The others sign too. The paper is dated January 13, 1777. It will be read by the men who make the laws. We do not know every detail of that day. But the paper itself still exists, and historians can read it.
story.think: Why do you think Prince Hall used the Revolution's own ideas about freedom in his petition?

lessons.title: Prince Hall's Boston
lessons.mainIdea: Prince Hall was a free Black man in Boston at a time when many Black people in Massachusetts were still enslaved.
reading: Boston in the 1770s was a busy port town. Ships came and went every day. Most people there were white. Some Black people in Boston were free. Many others were *enslaved*, which means they were owned by another person and forced to work.

Prince Hall was one of the free Black men of Boston. We know his name from letters, petitions and lodge records. We do not know for sure where he was born. Some writers say Barbados, but the *evidence* is not strong enough to be certain.

Historians are careful about facts like this. They use what the old papers show. When the papers do not agree, they say so. That is why this lesson says "we do not know" about his birthplace. Saying "we do not know" is an honest answer.

words.d: owned by another person and forced to work without freedom or pay
facts, papers or objects that help show whether something is true

look.title: Two Claims About a Birthplace
look.text: Claim A: "Prince Hall was born in Barbados." Claim B: "Prince Hall may have been born in Barbados, but no birth record proves it." Both claims are about the same man. Only one tells you how strong the evidence is.
look.prompt: Which claim is more careful? What word in it shows that the writer is not sure?

check.q: What does the word enslaved mean?
choices: Owned by another person and forced to work
Paid well for work on a ship
Living in a large port town
check.why: The reading says enslaved people were owned by another person and forced to work.

check.q: What do historians know for sure about where Prince Hall was born?
choices: They do not know for sure
check.why: The reading says some writers name Barbados, but the evidence is not strong enough to be certain.

check.q: How do we know Prince Hall's name today?
choices: From a statue made while he was alive
From a movie made long ago
From letters, petitions and lodge records
From a song his friends wrote
check.why: The reading says we know his name from letters, petitions and lodge records.

lessons.title: Fifteen Men Become Masons
lessons.mainIdea: In 1775, Prince Hall and fourteen other free Black men were made Masons in a lodge that belonged to a British army regiment.
reading: Freemasons are members of a brotherhood. They meet in a group called a *lodge*. A new member joins through a ceremony called an *initiation*. Masons use builders' tools, like the square, as symbols of good living.

In Boston, the Masons' lodges did not welcome Black men. So Prince Hall found another door. A British army *regiment* was in Boston. Its soldiers had their own lodge, called Lodge No. 441. A soldier named Sergeant John Batt belonged to it.

The usual date given is March 6, 1775. On that day, Prince Hall and fourteen other free Black men were made Masons in that army lodge. Fifteen men joined together. It was the start of a Black Masonic tradition that still lives today.

words.d: a local group of Masons, or the room where they meet
a ceremony that makes a person a new member of a group
a large group of soldiers in an army

look.title: Counting the Founders
look.text: Picture a lodge room lit by candles. Prince Hall stands in a line with fourteen other men. A soldier from the British army leads the ceremony. When it ends, fifteen new Masons stand in the room.
look.prompt: How many men were made Masons in all, counting Prince Hall? Why might joining as a group matter to them?

check.q: What is an initiation?
choices: A tool builders use to check corners
A ceremony that makes someone a new member
check.why: The reading says a new member joins through a ceremony called an initiation.

check.q: Whose lodge made Prince Hall and the others Masons?
choices: A lodge in a British army regiment
A lodge run by the Massachusetts lawmakers
check.why: The reading says a British army regiment in Boston had its own lodge, Lodge No. 441.

check.q: How many men in all were made Masons that day, counting Prince Hall?
check.why: Prince Hall and fourteen other men joined, so fifteen men became Masons.

lessons.title: A Lodge Without Full Papers
lessons.mainIdea: The army lodge soon left Boston, so the new Black Masons met as African Lodge, but they did not yet have a charter.
reading: The army lodge did not stay in Boston for long. Soldiers move where their army sends them. When the regiment left, its lodge went too. Prince Hall and his brothers stayed behind. They still wanted to meet as Masons. They called their group African Lodge.

But a lodge needs a *charter*. A charter is an official paper from a bigger Masonic body, called a *grand lodge*. It says a lodge is allowed to meet and to make new members. Without one, a lodge can do only part of its work.

African Lodge met anyway, with the limited permission it had. The members helped each other and kept records. They waited and hoped. Prince Hall decided to ask for a charter from far across the ocean.

words.d: an official paper that gives a group the right to meet and act
a Masonic body that leads many lodges and can give them charters

look.title: A Club Without a Paper
look.text: Imagine your class starts a reading club. You meet every week. But the school has not signed the paper that makes it an official club. You can still read together. You cannot yet use the library room or add new members the official way.
look.prompt: What could your club still do without the paper? What would change once the school signed it?

check.q: What happened to the army lodge when its regiment left Boston?
choices: It went away with the soldiers
check.why: The reading says that when the regiment left, its lodge went too.

check.q: What is a charter?
choices: A ship that crosses the ocean
An official paper that lets a lodge meet and make members
check.why: The reading says a charter is an official paper from a grand lodge that lets a lodge meet and make new members.

check.q: What name did Prince Hall's group use?
check.why: The reading says the men called their group African Lodge.

lessons.title: A Letter Across the Ocean
lessons.mainIdea: The Grand Lodge of England signed a charter for African Lodge No. 459 in 1784, and it finally reached Boston in 1787.
reading: Prince Hall wrote to the Grand Lodge of England in London. Letters went by sailing ship. Each trip across the Atlantic Ocean took weeks. Answers were slow. Prince Hall kept writing anyway.
At last, the Grand Lodge agreed. It signed a charter dated September 29, 1784. The paper named the group African Lodge No. 459. The number showed its place on the Grand Lodge's list of lodges.

Then the charter had to travel. It did not reach Boston until April 29, 1787. A ship captain named James Scott brought it. That is almost three years after it was signed. Prince Hall's patience had paid off.

words.d: the Masonic body in London that gave African Lodge its charter
the ability to wait calmly and keep trying

look.title: The Long Wait, Year by Year
look.cite: Prince Hall Grand Lodge histories; Wikipedia, African Lodge No. 459
look.prompt: How many years passed between the charter being signed and it reaching Boston?

check.q: Where did Prince Hall send his request for a charter?
choices: To the Grand Lodge of England in London
To the army in New York
check.why: The reading says he wrote to the Grand Lodge of England in London.

check.q: What was the full name on the charter?
check.why: The charter named the group African Lodge No. 459.

check.q: Look at the dates in the reading. How long did the charter take to reach Boston?
check.why: It was signed in September 1784 and reached Boston in April 1787, almost three years later.

lessons.title: 1775 or 1778?
lessons.mainIdea: A historian argued in 2026 that the fifteen men became Masons in 1778, not 1775, which shows history can be checked again.
reading: For a long time, Prince Hall Masons have given the date March 6, 1775. It is printed in many lodge histories. Many people celebrate it. But history is not frozen. New study can raise new questions.

In February 2026, a historian named Oscar Alleyne shared a paper in London. He studied Sergeant John Batt, the soldier who led the ceremony. Alleyne *argues* that the evidence points to March 6, 1778. That is three years later than the usual date.

Other historians will now look closely at his evidence. Some may agree. Some may not. For now, careful writers say "1775, though one historian now argues 1778." This is how history gets *revised*, or changed after new study.

words.d: gives reasons and evidence to support an idea
changed and improved after looking again

look.title: A New Paper About an Old Date
look.text: Alleyne studied the life of Sergeant John Batt. He argues that the records point to March 6, 1778, not 1775, as the day Prince Hall and the others were made Masons.
look.cite: Oscar Alleyne, "John Batt: Mercenary, Opportunist and Hero," Ars Quatuor Coronatorum 139, read in London, 2026
look.prompt: Which person did Alleyne study to learn about the date? Why would that person's records help?

check.q: What date do most lodge histories give for the start?
check.why: The reading says Prince Hall Masons have long given the date March 6, 1775.

check.q: What year does Oscar Alleyne argue for?
check.why: The reading says Alleyne argues the evidence points to March 6, 1778.

check.q: What does it mean when history is revised?
choices: It is changed after new study
check.why: The reading says revised means changed after new study.

sections.title: Speaking Up for Freedom and School

lessons.title: A Petition Against Slavery
lessons.mainIdea: In January 1777, Prince Hall and other Black men asked Massachusetts lawmakers to end slavery.
reading: In 1776, the Declaration of Independence said people have a right to liberty. Prince Hall heard those words. He saw that many Black people were still enslaved in Massachusetts. The words and the facts did not match.

So Prince Hall and other Black men wrote a *petition*. It was dated January 13, 1777. They sent it to the *legislature*, the group that makes a state's laws. They said Black people had a natural right to freedom, the same as everyone else.

The lawmakers did not end slavery that year. But the fight went on. In the early 1780s, Massachusetts courts ruled that slavery went against the state's new constitution. The petition is one early step in that long story.

words.d: a written request, often signed by many people, asking leaders to do something
the group of elected people who make a state's laws

look.title: What the 1777 Petition Asked
look.text: The signers said that they, like all people, had a natural right to freedom. They said this right came from God and was given equally to everyone. They asked the lawmakers to set enslaved people free.
look.cite: Prince Hall and others, petition to the Massachusetts legislature, January 13, 1777 (Massachusetts Archives)
look.prompt: What reason did the signers give for freedom? Find one idea that matches the Declaration of Independence.

check.q: What is a legislature?
choices: A group that makes a state's laws
check.why: The reading says the legislature is the group that makes a state's laws.

check.q: What did the 1777 petition ask for?
check.why: The petition asked Massachusetts lawmakers to end slavery.

check.q: What happened to slavery in Massachusetts in the early 1780s?
choices: Courts ruled it went against the state constitution
check.why: The reading says courts ruled that slavery went against the state's new constitution.

lessons.title: A Petition for Schools
lessons.mainIdea: In 1787, Prince Hall asked for schools for Black children, and when that failed, the community opened its own school.
reading: Black families in Boston paid *taxes*, just like white families. Taxes are money people pay to the government. Some of that money paid for free public schools. But Black children were kept out of those schools.

On October 17, 1787, Prince Hall and others sent a petition about this. They asked for schools their children could attend. The lawmakers said no. The families were paying for schools their children could not use.

So the community acted on its own. In 1798, an African School opened in the home of Primus Hall, Prince Hall's son. In 1803 it moved to a shop on Belknap Street. Families built what the town would not give them.

words.d: money people must pay to the government for shared things like roads and schools
a group of people who live near each other and help each other

look.title: The Parents' Complaint
look.text: The petitioners said they paid taxes like other people in Boston. They said their children still could not go to the free schools. They feared their children would grow up without learning, only because they were Black.
look.cite: Prince Hall and others, petition for schooling, October 17, 1787 (Massachusetts Archives)
look.prompt: Why did the parents think the rule was unfair? Use the word taxes in your answer.

check.q: What did Black families pay that helped fund Boston's schools?
check.why: The reading says Black families paid taxes, and some tax money paid for public schools.

check.q: What did the lawmakers do with the 1787 school petition?
choices: They made Prince Hall a teacher
check.why: The reading says the lawmakers said no.

check.q: Where did the African School open in 1798?
choices: In the home of Prince Hall's son, Primus Hall
check.why: The reading says the school opened in the home of Primus Hall, Prince Hall's son.

lessons.title: Speaking for His Neighbors
lessons.mainIdea: Prince Hall used petitions and speeches to protect his neighbors and give them hope.
reading: In early 1788, three free Black men from Boston were hired to work on a ship. Then they were locked below deck. The ship sailed away. The plan was to sell them into slavery. Their families were afraid.

Prince Hall wrote a petition about the men. Other people in Boston spoke up too. On March 26, 1788, Massachusetts passed a law against the slave trade. The law also offered help to families of people taken this way. Speaking up had made a difference.

Years later, in June 1797, Prince Hall gave a speech to his lodge. It is called a *Charge*. He spoke about the insults his brothers faced on Boston's streets. He also shared *hope*, from news that enslaved people in Haiti had won their freedom.

words.d: a serious speech that gives advice to members of a lodge
a feeling that good things can happen in the future

look.title: Prince Hall's 1797 Charge
look.text: Prince Hall told his lodge brothers to be patient and strong. He named the insults they met in the streets of Boston. He pointed to the people of Haiti, who had broken free from slavery, as a sign of hope.
look.cite: Prince Hall, A Charge Delivered to the African Lodge, June 24, 1797, at Menotomy (Boston, 1797)
look.prompt: Prince Hall named a hard thing and a hopeful thing. What was each one?

check.q: What law did Massachusetts pass on March 26, 1788?
choices: A law against the slave trade
A law opening schools to all
check.why: The reading says Massachusetts passed a law against the slave trade on that date.

check.q: What is a Charge in a lodge?
choices: A serious speech that gives advice
check.why: The reading says the Charge was a speech Prince Hall gave to his lodge.

check.q: Where did Prince Hall point for hope in his 1797 speech?
check.why: He shared hope from news that enslaved people in Haiti had won their freedom.

lessons.title: A Lodge That Grew
lessons.mainIdea: African Lodge became independent in 1827, and lodges named for Prince Hall spread across the country, including Illinois.
reading: In 1813, the Grand Lodges of England joined into one. African Lodge was left off the new list of lodges. Its members kept meeting. In 1827, African Lodge said it was *independent*. It would lead itself.

New Black lodges grew from this start. In time, people called them *Prince Hall Masonry*, to honor the founder. Lodges spread from Boston to other states. Each state came to have its own Prince Hall grand lodge.

Illinois is part of this story. North Star Lodge No. 12 was set up in Chicago in 1852. Lodges followed in Alton and Springfield. In 1867, the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Illinois was formed at Springfield.

words.d: free to make its own decisions, not led by another group
the Masonic lodges that trace their start to Prince Hall and African Lodge

look.title: Early Prince Hall Lodges in Illinois
look.cite: Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Illinois, lodge history
look.prompt: Which Illinois city had the first lodge on this list? How many years later was the Grand Lodge formed?

check.q: What did African Lodge say about itself in 1827?
choices: That it would move to London
That it was part of the army
check.why: The reading says African Lodge said it was independent in 1827.

check.q: Why is it called Prince Hall Masonry?
choices: To honor its founder, Prince Hall
Because it meets in a hall
check.why: The reading says the lodges were named to honor the founder, Prince Hall.

check.q: Where was the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Illinois formed in 1867?
check.why: The reading says it was formed at Springfield in 1867.

lessons.title: Recognition Came Slowly
lessons.mainIdea: For many years white grand lodges refused to accept Prince Hall lodges, but since 1989 most of them do.
reading: For a long time, most white grand lodges in America would not *recognize* Prince Hall Masons. To recognize means to accept another group as true members. Some even called Prince Hall lodges fake. Race was a big reason.

That began to change in 1989. The Grand Lodge of Connecticut became the first mainstream grand lodge in the United States to recognize Prince Hall Masonry. Since then, most other state grand lodges have done the same.

Prince Hall lodges did much more than wait. Scholars such as Theda Skocpol show they trained *leaders*. Members learned to run meetings and manage money. Many lodges also helped pay for the fight for civil rights. Women joined Prince Hall Eastern Star chapters, starting in 1874.

words.d: to accept another group as real and equal members
people who guide a group and help it make choices

look.title: Two Clubs, One Name
look.text: Two clubs in the same town both study the same book and use the same rules. One club says the other is not a real club. The only big difference is who the members are. Years later, the first club changes its mind.
look.prompt: How is this like the story of Prince Hall lodges? What finally changed in 1989?

check.q: What does recognize mean in this lesson?
choices: To see someone across a room
To accept another group as true members
check.why: The reading says to recognize means to accept another group as true members.

check.q: Which grand lodge was the first mainstream one to recognize Prince Hall Masonry?
check.why: The reading says the Grand Lodge of Connecticut was first, in 1989.

check.q: What does Theda Skocpol's research show about Prince Hall lodges?
choices: They met only once a year
They trained leaders and helped the civil rights fight
They were part of the British army
check.why: The reading says scholars such as Skocpol show the lodges trained leaders and helped pay for the civil rights fight.

lessons.title: Papers in a Chicago Library
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's Woodson Regional Library keeps an open archive of Prince Hall Masonry papers that anyone can study.
reading: On South Halsted Street in Chicago stands the Woodson Regional Library. It is part of the Chicago Public Library. Inside is the Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection. It is one of the largest collections on Black history and culture in the Midwest.

One part of it is the Prince Hall Freemasonry Archives. An *archive* is a place that keeps old papers safe. This one fills 16 boxes. The papers run from 1902 to 2006. Two men gave them to the library in April 1997.
The papers show Black lodge life in Chicago in the 1900s. There are no special limits on who can study them. A student with a question can use real *primary sources*, just as historians do.

words.d: a place that keeps old papers and records safe so people can study them
papers, objects or pictures made by people who lived at the time

look.title: The Prince Hall Archive by the Numbers
look.unit: count, feet or year (see each row)
look.cite: Chicago Public Library, Prince Hall Freemasonry Archives finding aid (collection 1997/03)
look.prompt: About how many years do the papers cover? Why might a long span help a historian?

check.q: What is an archive?
choices: A place that keeps old papers safe
check.why: The reading says an archive is a place that keeps old papers safe.

check.q: Which library holds the Prince Hall Freemasonry Archives?
choices: The Woodson Regional Library in Chicago
check.why: The reading says the archive is at the Woodson Regional Library, part of the Chicago Public Library.

check.q: Which of these is a primary source?
choices: A cartoon made last week about 1900
check.why: A primary source is made by people who lived at the time, like a lodge paper from 1950.

choices: A free Black man in Boston who founded African Lodge
A ship captain who carried letters
review.why: Prince Hall was a free Black man in Boston who led African Lodge.

review.q: In what kind of lodge were Prince Hall and fourteen other men made Masons?
choices: A lodge in a British army regiment
review.why: They joined through Lodge No. 441, which belonged to a British army regiment.

review.q: Why did African Lodge need a charter?
choices: To be allowed to meet and make members officially
review.why: A charter is an official paper that lets a lodge meet and make new members.

review.q: The charter was signed in 1784. When did it reach Boston?
review.why: Captain James Scott brought the charter to Boston in April 1787.

review.q: How are the 1777 petition and the 1787 petition different?
choices: The first asked to end slavery; the second asked for schools
The first asked for schools; the second asked for a charter
Both asked for a new lodge
review.why: The 1777 petition asked for an end to slavery, and the 1787 petition asked for schools for Black children.

review.q: What does Oscar Alleyne's 2026 paper show about history?
choices: That old dates can never change
That Prince Hall lived in Chicago
That historians can check dates again and argue for new ones
That the charter was never sent
review.why: Alleyne argues for 1778 instead of 1775, showing that history can be revised.

choices: The Grand Lodge of Connecticut recognized Prince Hall Masonry
review.why: In 1989 Connecticut's grand lodge became the first mainstream one to recognize Prince Hall Masonry.

review.q: Why might a Chicago student visit the Woodson Regional Library?
choices: To see the ship that carried the charter
To study Prince Hall lodge papers from 1902 to 2006
review.why: The library's Harsh Collection holds the Prince Hall Freemasonry Archives, open for study.
